design_detail: Systematic review with mixed-effects meta-regression of 87 cohort studies (523 relative-risk estimates) of alcohol consumption and all-cause mortality, testing whether ‘abstainer biases’ (former and/or occasional drinkers counted in the abstainer reference group) and other study characteristics explain the J-shaped curve. Three strategies: all studies pooled with study-level covariates (Tables 2 and 3); studies stratified by type of abstainer bias (Table 4); and a subset of ‘higher quality’ studies with strictly defined lifetime abstainers (Table 5). Protocol approved as a US National Institutes of Health R01 grant application, presented as online Appendix A (not read); no registry record.
can_establish: How much the pooled association between low-volume drinking and all-cause mortality in published cohort studies (to 2014) depends on how each study defined its abstainer reference group and on other study characteristics, and what studies with strictly defined lifetime abstainers show.
cannot_establish: Whether low-volume drinking causes or prevents deaths (the data are observational and the adjustment is at study level, that is ecological); a pooled risk that applies to any defined population (the adjusted estimates are model predictions whose covariate reference levels are not stated); outcomes other than all-cause mortality; the shape of the curve below 25 g/day (a single low-volume category); or the absence of a modest effect in either direction (the adjusted low-volume interval, 0.88 to 1.07, includes both).

sample.recruitment: Database search: PubMed (last searched 25 February 2015) and Web of Science for English-language articles published up to 31 December 2014, plus the reference lists of two earlier meta-analyses (Fillmore et al., 2006; Ronksley et al., 2011). 2,662 records identified, 87 studies included (Method › Data sources; Study selection; Results › Study selection; Figure 1, an image).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original English-language peer-reviewed cohort studies quantifying all-cause mortality by level of alcohol consumption in human populations, any sex, age, ethnic group or region. Excluded: studies whose mortality outcome could not be separated from morbidity, and samples defined by pre-existing illness or poor health. Where a cohort had several publications, the most recent or the most comprehensive in its handling of bias and confounding was used (Method › Inclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Of the 87 studies, 30 reported separate estimates for men and women, 31 men only, 7 women only, 19 both combined; median cohort age at intake 54.5 years (SD 10.5); 77 from North America, Europe or Australia and 10 from Japan, China or India; mean follow-up 13.4 years (SD 6.6); 34 excluded unhealthy participants; 64 used an intake measure coded as adequate (Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English only, two databases, no grey literature or registries, search ending in December 2014. The included cohorts are mostly from high-income, mainly white populations. Choice of one publication per cohort, and the rules for converting categories to grams, could change estimates; per-study data are in online appendices B and D (not read).

exposure.measurement: Mean daily intake in grams of ethanol at baseline, self-reported in every primary study, converted from each study's categories with the study's drink size or a country-specific estimate (8 g in the UK to 19.75 g in Japan) and category midpoints; open-ended top categories set at the lower bound plus three quarters of the width of the next-lower category. An intake measure was coded ‘adequate’ if quantity and frequency were assessed over at least one week (64 of 87 studies) (Method › Measures of alcohol consumption; Quality assessment).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories in g/day: lifetime abstainers (reference, strictly zero lifetime consumption); former drinkers (now completely abstaining); occasional, less than 1.30 (up to one drink a week); low volume 1.30 to 24.9 (up to two drinks); medium 25 to 44.9 (up to four); high 45 to 64.9 (up to six); higher, 65 or more. Low volume was set in advance from the Australian NHMRC limit of 20 g/day and operationalized as up to 24 g because studies reported whole drinks (Method › Measures of alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph; Analyses, 4th paragraph). For orientation, 25 g/day is 175 g/week (editors' arithmetic).
exposure.polysubstance: Whether the primary study controlled for smoking is coded as a study-level covariate; no other substance is considered.

comparison.controls: Each study's own ‘abstainer’ group: in 74 of 87 studies it included former and/or occasional drinkers (41 both, 24 former only, 9 occasional only); 13 studies used strictly defined lifetime abstainers. Alternative reference: occasional drinkers (Table 2, right-hand columns; method in Appendix A, Box 1, not read).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Study-level covariates in the meta-regression: median age at intake, sex, mainly Caucasian population or not, adequacy of the intake measure, former-drinker bias and occasional-drinker bias (six-covariate model), then also follow-up years, exclusion of ill participants and whether the study controlled for race and smoking (full model).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within the cohorts, drinking history before baseline, reasons for abstaining, earlier health, socio-economic position, diet and physical activity are handled only by whatever each study adjusted for; apart from smoking and race control, these are not among the meta-regression covariates.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality as reported by each cohort: hazard ratios or rate ratios used as relative risks (RR), RRs computed from rates where only rates were reported, and estimates recalculated against abstainers when a study used occasional drinkers as its reference (Method › Summary measures of outcome).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death is an objective outcome; ascertainment methods of the cohorts are not described.
outcomes.operationalization: RR of death for each drinking category against the study's reference group, natural-log transformed; summary RRs are inverse-variance-weighted mixed-model estimates (fixed effects for drinking category and covariates, random intercept for study).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, but six drinking categories estimated in at least ten models (Tables 2 to 5), each tested at p < .05 with t tests; covariates entered on bivariable p < .20.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two trained reviewers read all titles; abstracts were then reviewed (by whom is not stated) and full texts checked for eligibility with cross-checking by senior investigators; two reviewers extracted and coded the data, disagreements resolved by discussion, and the coding was double-checked by the first two authors (Method › Study selection; Data extraction).

analysis.effect_sizes: All RRs for all-cause mortality. Table 2 (weighted for precision and between-study variation only), against each study's abstainers: former drinkers 1.22 (95% CI 1.14 to 1.31), 21 studies, 42 estimates, I2 65%; occasional 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), 15 studies, I2 61%; low volume 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90), 81 studies, 229 estimates, I2 65%; medium 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00), p = .031, I2 80%; high 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17), I2 82%; higher 1.29 (1.22 to 1.36), I2 83%; all drinkers combined 1.00 (0.85 to 1.17). Against occasional drinkers: abstainers 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27); former 1.45 (1.33 to 1.59); low 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10); medium 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22); high 1.33 (1.24 to 1.44); higher 1.52 (1.40 to 1.66); all drinkers 1.24 (1.08 to 1.42). Table 3, six covariates: former 1.26 (1.17 to 1.35); occasional 0.86 (0.80 to 0.92); low 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94); medium 0.98 (0.92 to 1.04); high 1.13 (1.06 to 1.20); higher 1.32 (1.23 to 1.41). Table 3, all covariates: former 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54); occasional 0.95 (0.85 to 1.05); low 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07); medium 1.07 (0.97 to 1.18); high 1.24 (1.12 to 1.37); higher 1.44 (1.30 to 1.60); all drinkers 1.15 (0.97 to 1.36). Table 4, 13 studies with lifetime abstainers only (adjusted for median age, sex and country): former 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57); occasional 0.94 (0.71 to 1.25), 4 estimates; low 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), 50 estimates; medium 0.95 (0.80 to 1.13); high 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32); higher 1.42 (1.15 to 1.75); in the three groups of studies with abstainer biases, low volume 0.91 (0.83 to 1.00), 0.86 (0.78 to 0.95) and 0.86 (0.82 to 0.91). Table 5, seven higher-quality studies against lifetime abstainers (sampling and between-study variation only): low 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), higher 1.58 (1.05 to 2.38), former 1.14 (0.77 to 1.69); without the influential Friesema et al. (2007) study: low 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15), medium 1.29 (1.06 to 1.56), former 1.31 (1.11 to 1.55), higher 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27). Egger tests: no significant publication bias for any category.
analysis.covariates: Study-level only: median age at intake (continuous), sex, mainly Caucasian population or not, adequacy of the intake measure, former-drinker bias, occasional-drinker bias; full model adds follow-up years, exclusion of ill participants and whether race and smoking were controlled in the study. Candidates were screened by bivariable p < .20 and pruned for intercorrelations above .30. No significant interaction with median age, sex or Caucasian status. The paper does not state at which covariate values (reference levels or averages) the adjusted category RRs are evaluated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the protocol was first approved as an NIH R01 grant application (Award 1RO1AAO19939-02) and present it as online Appendix A (not read); there is no registry record. PRISMA followed (Method › Overall approach).
analysis.selective_reporting: Results excluding outliers are said to be the same but are not reported; forest plots, influence analyses and per-study data are in Appendices B to F (not read). The Discussion emphasizes the Table 5 estimates after removal of the influential study. Outcome-specific results (CHD) are outside this paper.
analysis.power: Strata are small where the conclusion rests: 4 occasional-drinker estimates in the bias-free studies, 6 or 7 higher-quality studies (low-volume interval 0.62 to 1.29 with Friesema et al.). The authors argue that two estimates per covariate suffice for linear regression (Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling 87 cohorts with only precision and between-study variation accounted for reproduced the J-shape (low volume RR 0.86, occasional 0.84, against each study's abstainers). Adding study-level covariates for abstainer biases and other characteristics moved the low-volume RR to 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) while former drinkers (1.38) and people drinking 45 g/day or more (1.24; 1.44) stayed at higher risk. In the 13 studies with strict lifetime abstainers, low-volume RR was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06); in the higher-quality subset, 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), or 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) after removing one study. Occasional drinkers had RRs like low-volume drinkers in every model, and against occasional drinkers low-volume RR was 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10) while abstainers had 1.19.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that low-volume consumption “has no net mortality benefit compared with lifetime abstention or occasional drinking”. Gaps: (1) non-significance is read as absence: the fully adjusted interval (0.88 to 1.07) is compatible with up to 12% lower or 7% higher mortality, and in the bias-free stratum the point estimate is 0.90; (2) the adjusted RRs come from an ecological meta-regression, with covariates chosen partly by bivariable p-values and evaluated at unstated reference levels, so they are not the risk in any defined set of studies; (3) the higher-quality conclusion leans on the analysis that drops an influential study after the fact (both versions are non-significant); (4) the occasional-drinker reference, which the authors favour, also shows abstainers at higher risk (1.19), which fits abstainer bias but confirms that the choice of reference group drives the conclusion; (5) the Discussion concedes that even the 13 bias-free studies had other serious problems that could bias results in either direction. The paper's own summary, that a sceptical position about net benefit is warranted, is proportionate to these results, and the authors are open that occasional-drinker bias could not be confirmed.

timeline.event: Shaper et al.: the ‘sick quitter’ explanation of the U-shaped curve in British men (cited in the background).
Naimi et al.: 27 of 30 potential confounders of coronary heart disease more common among US non-drinkers than moderate drinkers (cited; Naimi is a co-author of this review).

Fillmore et al.: the original meta-analysis classifying studies by abstainer definition, whose codebook this review refines (Stockwell and Chikritzhs are co-authors). The project list also holds Di Castelnuovo et al. (2006), a J-curve meta-analysis of 34 studies, which this review does not cite.

Ronksley et al. meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes, whose reference list was searched and whose conclusion is cited as the case for advising abstainers to drink (carded in this round by another reader).
Holmes et al. Mendelian randomization study, cited in the conclusions as consistent with this review (carded in this round by another reader).
Chikritzhs et al. editorial arguing the protective hypothesis had collapsed, cited in this review's first sentence; three of its authors wrote this review (card sc_chikritzhs_2015, this round).
Same issue of the journal: commentaries by Greenfield, by Connor and by Rehm, Roerecke and Room, with the authors' response (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 77:199–207; titles from PubMed, not read).

Letter by Barrett-Connor and 16 co-signatories, ‘Comments on Moderate Alcohol Consumption and Mortality’, letters by Gow and by Braillon, and a reply by Stockwell, Chikritzhs, Naimi and Zhao whose title frames the critique as coming from ISFAR and industry sympathizers (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 77:834–841; not read).
Commentary by Xuan in Evidence-Based Medicine (21:194), listed on PubMed (not read).
Wood et al. individual-participant analysis of 599,912 current drinkers, which avoids the abstainer reference group altogether (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Zhao et al. update by the same group (107 studies, the same 87 plus 20): fully adjusted low-volume RR 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).
Stockwell et al. review of study characteristics that may bias low-volume mortality estimates, on the project list (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The review is the base dataset of a series of meta-analyses by one group. Its central result, that counting former drinkers in the reference group lowers drinkers' relative risks and that the low-volume association moves towards 1 when study characteristics are taken into account, was reproduced by the group's own update (Zhao et al., 2023), which is not independent and whose adjusted estimate (0.93, 0.85 to 1.01) sits further from 1 than this one. Critiques and replies were published in the same journal in 2016 and have not been read. The question cannot be settled by study-level meta-regression; individual-participant analyses with lifetime drinking histories and genetic studies (carded separately) approach it differently.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health Award # 1RO1AAO19939-02, initially held by the late Kaye Middleton Fillmore, principal investigator (Footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the PMC version; only the funding footnote.
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addictions Research of BC, University of Victoria; National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University; Institute for Scientific Analysis, San Francisco; Boston University Schools of Medicine and Public Health. Stockwell and Chikritzhs co-authored Fillmore et al. (2006), whose classification this review refines, and three of the authors (Chikritzhs, Stockwell, Naimi) had argued in a 2015 editorial that the protective hypothesis had collapsed, so the authors test a position they had already taken in print. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant analysis of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories, so that former drinkers can be reassigned to the levels they drank, with strictly defined lifetime abstainers, repeated intake measures and common adjustment for socio-economic and health confounders; or a long-term randomized trial of low-volume drinking against abstention.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: General-population cohorts, alcohol consumption by level, abstainers or occasional drinkers as comparators, all-cause mortality.

Provisional: the authors state the protocol was approved as an NIH grant application and give it as online Appendix A, which was not read, so whether it specified the question, search, criteria and bias assessment cannot be checked. There is no registry record.
The question is defined as one about biases in prospective cohort studies, so cohorts are the designs at issue.

Two databases with the key words printed and reference lists of two meta-analyses, but English only without justification, no grey literature, no registries and no experts consulted; search ended February 2015 for a 2016 paper.

Two trained reviewers read all titles, and full-text eligibility was cross-checked by senior investigators; who reviewed the abstracts, and whether screening was independent, is not stated, so this is a close call.
Two reviewers extracted and coded all studies, disagreements resolved with the investigators, coding double-checked by the first two authors.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons were documented at each stage and summarized in the flow chart (an image), but no list of excluded studies is given or mentioned; the appendices were not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article gives only aggregate characteristics (Table 1); study-by-study details are in Appendix B (Tables B1 to B4) and Appendix D (Table D1), not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No formal tool, but each study was coded for the selection and misclassification problems at issue (former and occasional drinkers in the reference group, exclusion of ill participants, age at intake) and for confounder control (smoking, race) and intake measurement; selection of reported results was not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Inverse-variance-weighted mixed models with a random study intercept, the combination justified by the aim; reported hazard or rate ratios were used and crude rates converted only when nothing else was reported. Met on balance, a close call: whether the most-adjusted estimate was taken is not stated, the correlation between categories sharing a reference group is handled only by the random intercept, and the adjusted RRs are evaluated at unstated covariate levels.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The review's purpose: bias covariates in the meta-regression, stratification by abstainer bias and a higher-quality subset.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Results are interpreted through the bias analyses, and the Discussion notes remaining problems in the bias-free studies.
Q and I2 reported (all above 50%), meta-regression and stratification explore sources, and the reduced heterogeneity in the higher-quality subset is reported (Appendix F).
Funnel plot (Appendix C) and Egger tests for each category and for all drinkers; no significant bias found.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding is reported, but there is no statement of the authors' competing interests or how they were managed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items fail (item 4, English-only search without justification; item 7, no list of excluded studies), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; item 2 is provisional (appendix not read) but cannot change the rating. This rates how far the pooled numbers can be taken as an unbiased summary, not the value of the idea: the review is transparent about its coding, tests a clearly stated hypothesis in three ways and reports unadjusted estimates beside adjusted ones. The card may be cited for the finding that abstainer definitions and study characteristics move the low-volume RR from about 0.86 towards 1, for the higher mortality of former drinkers and of drinkers of 45 g/day or more in every model, and for the counts of studies by type of reference group. It should not be cited for a demonstrated absence of benefit, or for any adjusted RR as the risk in a real population.

key_findings.finding: 87 cohort studies were included from 2,662 records (PubMed and Web of Science, English-language articles published to 31 December 2014, plus reference lists of two earlier meta-analyses): 523 relative-risk estimates from 3,998,626 participants with 367,103 deaths.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Method; Method › Data sources; Results › Study selection; Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias

key_findings.finding: Of the 87 studies, 65 counted former drinkers in the abstainer reference group and 50 counted occasional drinkers (41 both, 24 former only, 9 occasional only); only 13 studies (127 estimates) used strictly defined lifetime abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Summary of evidence, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias

key_findings.finding: Weighted only for precision and between-study variation, against each study's abstainers: low-volume drinkers (1.30 to 24.9 g/day) RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.90), occasional drinkers (under 1.30 g/day) 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), former drinkers 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31), medium volume (25 to 44.9 g/day) 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00), high (45 to 64.9) 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17), higher (65 or more) 1.29 (1.22 to 1.36). Heterogeneity significant in every category, I2 61% to 84%; Egger tests showed no publication bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality with limited adjustment, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: With occasional drinkers as the reference: abstainers RR 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27), low volume 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10), medium 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22), high 1.33 (1.24 to 1.44), higher 1.52 (1.40 to 1.66), former drinkers 1.45 (1.33 to 1.59).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality with limited adjustment, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, right-hand columns

key_findings.finding: Fully adjusted meta-regression (study-level covariates: median age, sex, Caucasian population, intake-measure adequacy, former- and occasional-drinker bias, follow-up years, exclusion of ill participants, control for race and smoking), against abstainers: former drinkers 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54), occasional 0.95 (0.85 to 1.05), low volume 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07), medium 1.07 (0.97 to 1.18), high 1.24 (1.12 to 1.37), higher 1.44 (1.30 to 1.60). With the six first covariates only, low volume was 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality after adjustment, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: The covariate values at which these model estimates are evaluated are not stated.

key_findings.finding: As the bias and quality covariates are removed from the full model, the low-volume RR falls from 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) to 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90); the authors' Appendix E is said to confirm the importance of former-drinker bias and to suggest that occasional-drinker bias matters less.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality after adjustment, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 caption
key_findings.note: Figure 3 is an image; intermediate values were not extracted. Appendix E not read.

key_findings.finding: In the 13 studies with strictly defined lifetime abstainers (adjusted for median age, sex and country): low volume RR 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), 50 estimates; occasional 0.94 (0.71 to 1.25), 4 estimates; medium 0.95 (0.80 to 1.13); high 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32); higher 1.42 (1.15 to 1.75); former drinkers 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57). In the three groups of studies with abstainer biases, low volume was 0.91 (0.83 to 1.00) in the 41 studies with both former- and occasional-drinker bias, 0.86 (0.78 to 0.95) in the 24 with former-drinker bias only and 0.86 (0.82 to 0.91) in the 9 with occasional-drinker bias only; the bias-free point estimate (0.90) is about the same as that of the studies with both biases (0.91), with a wider interval.
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimates of all-cause mortality risk among studies stratified by abstainer bias; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Seven higher-quality studies (lifetime abstainers only, adequate intake measure, median age under 60 at intake and at least 55 at follow-up), against lifetime abstainers: low volume RR 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), medium 1.08 (0.72 to 1.62), high 0.95 (0.62 to 1.46), higher 1.58 (1.05 to 2.38), former 1.14 (0.77 to 1.69). Leave-one-out analysis found Friesema et al. (2007) highly influential (6 of its estimates were outliers); without it: low volume 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15), medium 1.29 (1.06 to 1.56), high 1.07 (0.83 to 1.36), former 1.31 (1.11 to 1.55), higher 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27), with I2 below 50% for former, low and medium categories.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis of higher quality studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5
key_findings.note: Table 5 estimates are adjusted for sampling variability and between-study variation only. In the bias-free and higher-quality subsets the 45 to under 65 g category was never significantly raised (1.11 in key finding 6; 0.95 and 1.07 here), while 25 to under 45 g was in the model without Friesema et al. (1.29): in these small subsets the intake at which risk rises is not well defined.

key_findings.finding: Outliers (log RR beyond the category mean plus or minus 2 SD): 11 estimates below (RR 0.1 to 0.46) and 18 above (1.89 to 4.57); removing them made no substantive difference, so all models include them. No significant effect modification by median age, sex or Caucasian population.

Definitions: lifetime abstention strictly zero consumption, excluding any occasional lifetime or past-year drinking; abstainers in studies that measured typical weekly or monthly drinking were assumed to include occasional drinkers; intake measure adequate if quantity and frequency covered at least one week.

The authors' limitations: imperfect, mostly under-reported self-reported intake and unreliable classification of lifetime abstainers; few studies in some stratified analyses; too few studies controlling for heavy episodic drinking to examine it; findings apply to all-cause mortality only.

The authors conclude that counting former drinkers among abstainers biases drinkers' RRs downward, that bias from occasional drinkers could not be confirmed, and that if occasional drinkers were the reference there would be no evidence of protection for any drinking category; they recommend excluding former and occasional drinkers from abstainer groups and considering occasional drinkers as the reference.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 has 87 estimates with Friesema et al. and 77 without, so removing that study removed 10 estimates (2 former, 4 low, 2 medium, 2 high), whereas the text says the study contributed 8 estimates, 6 of them outliers (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Meta-analysis of higher quality studies, 1st paragraph; Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition of the higher-quality subset cannot be reconciled from the article; the without-Friesema estimates should be quoted with that caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of studies is inconsistent across tables and text: former drinkers come from 21 studies in Table 2 but 20 in Table 3 (42 estimates in both); occasional drinkers from 15 studies in Tables 2 and 3 but 17 in the Discussion; the bias-free studies give 4 occasional-drinker estimates in Table 4 but three in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Tables 2 to 4; Discussion › Summary of evidence, 9th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the estimates, but counts of studies should be taken from the tables, with the discrepancy noted.

reporting_issues.issue: Estimate totals in Table 4 do not match Table 1: the studies with both biases total 178 estimates in Table 4 against 180 in Table 1, and those with occasional-drinker bias only 69 against 76 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Some estimates are unaccounted for in the stratified models.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 percentages: the 194 estimates from cohorts aged 50 to 59 are printed as 39.09% of 523 (it is 37.09%; editors' arithmetic); the sex rows count 117 studies under a column headed N = 87 because 30 studies report men and women separately.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list four criteria for the higher-quality subset (lifetime abstainers only, adequate intake measure, smoking controlled, median age under 60 at intake and at least 55 at follow-up), but the Table 5 footnote omits smoking control.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Method › Synthesis of results; Table 5 footnote
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether smoking control was applied as a selection criterion.

reporting_issues.issue: The row ‘All drinkers combined’ pools all estimates including former drinkers (its estimate counts equal the totals with the former-drinker estimates), which the tables do not say.
reporting_issues.consequence: That row is not an estimate for current drinkers and should not be cited as one.

reporting_issues.issue: The covariate values (reference levels or averages) at which the adjusted category RRs in Table 3 are computed are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The fully adjusted RRs, including the headline 0.97, describe an unspecified hypothetical study; claims should present them as model-based estimates.
